about: Patients, Communities and Healthcare Year 1 (MEDI40004) is a core 10-credit module of Imperial's MBBS/BSc Medicine that runs from autumn to summer (programme specification 2026-27); the programme specification says patient contact in Years 1 and 2 is delivered through the PCH modules, and Imperial's primary care teaching page describes PCH 1 as students' first contact with patients at medical school. Groups of four or eight spend eight Thursdays between October and March in a GP practice, doing patient conversations, sitting in GP clinics, a community survey project and small-group tutorials, and exploring the biological, psychological and social sides of illness; the specification adds that patients may also be seen at home and in hospital. Imperial does not publish a topic-by-topic syllabus, so the topics in this pack are built from the official description and the programme's outcomes on communication, ethics and law, and population health, using standard UK material. A 2019 Imperial GP-teaching post said PCH was assessed by workplace-based assessments and the survey project; the 2026-27 specification confirms only that workplace-based assessments begin in Year 1 and that every module must be passed.

notes.h: Health, illness and the biopsychosocial model
notes.body:
Patients, Communities and Healthcare asks you to look at illness as more than a fault in the body. The organising idea is the biopsychosocial model, and much of what you see in the GP practice can be explained with a small set of concepts from medical sociology.

Biomedical versus biopsychosocial
- The biomedical model explains illness as a departure from normal biological function and aims treatment at the lesion. It is powerful, but it is reductionist: it struggles with symptoms that have no clear pathology, and with why two people with the same disease do so differently.
- George Engel set out the biopsychosocial model in the journal Science in 1977 ("The need for a new medical model"). Biological factors (genes, pathology), psychological factors (beliefs, mood, coping, behaviour) and social factors (family, work, money, housing, culture) interact to shape the onset, course and outcome of illness.
- Worked example: two men have the same lumbar disc prolapse. One has an office job, a supportive partner and expects the pain to settle. The other is a self-employed labourer in debt who fears he will be paralysed and so avoids moving. The biology is the same; the disability, time off work and recovery are likely to be very different.

Disease, illness and sickness
- Disease: the professional's frame, a pathological abnormality that can be detected and measured.
- Illness: the person's own experience of feeling unwell.
- Sickness: the social status of being recognised as ill by others (for example being signed off work).
You can have disease without illness (symptomless high blood pressure) and illness without any disease that tests can find.

The sick role (Talcott Parsons, The Social System, 1951)
- Rights: the sick person is excused normal social duties, and is not blamed for being ill.
- Obligations: they should want to get better, and should seek technically competent help and cooperate with it.
- Criticisms: it fits short acute illness better than chronic illness or disability; it pictures a passive patient; and it ignores conditions where people are blamed or disbelieved.

Deciding to see a doctor
- Most symptoms are managed at home without professional help; the cases doctors see are the tip of a "symptom iceberg".
- Irving Zola (1973) described non-medical triggers that push people to consult: an interpersonal crisis, interference with social relationships, being told to go by others ("sanctioning"), interference with work or physical activity, and setting a deadline ("if it is not better by Monday...").
- Lay beliefs and lay referral (family, friends, the internet) shape whether and when people come.

Chronic illness and stigma
- Michael Bury (1982) called chronic illness a "biographical disruption": it breaks taken-for-granted assumptions about the future and forces people to rethink their identity, relationships and plans.
- Erving Goffman (Stigma, 1963) described stigma as an attribute that deeply discredits a person. He distinguished the discredited (the difference is visible or already known) from the discreditable (the difference can be hidden, so the person must manage information about it).
- Graham Scambler and Anthony Hopkins (1986), studying people with epilepsy, separated enacted stigma (actual discrimination) from felt stigma (shame and fear of discrimination). Felt stigma was often the more disruptive, because people restricted their own lives to avoid rejection.

Why it matters on placement
In patient conversations and home visits you will meet people who have lived with illness for years. Ask what they think is wrong, how it affects work, family and mood, and what matters most to them. That is the biopsychosocial model in practice, and it links directly to the communication skills and health inequalities topics.

Exam tips: define each term precisely, attach a named thinker and date, and apply the concept to a concrete patient rather than just listing "biological, psychological, social".

notes.h: Talking with patients: communication and patient conversations
notes.body:
Patient conversations are your first real clinical encounters. In Year 1 the aim is not to diagnose but to hear a person's story, understand what illness means to them, and practise the skills that every later consultation depends on.

Before you start
- Introduce yourself by name and say that you are a medical student. Explain the purpose and roughly how long it will take.
- Get the patient's agreement, and tell them they can stop at any point.
- Choose a private space and sit at a comfortable distance and level.

The Calgary-Cambridge guide
The most widely taught framework in UK medical schools comes from Kurtz and Silverman (1996), developed with Draper (1998). It has five tasks in sequence:
- Initiating the session (greeting, establishing the reasons for the visit)
- Gathering information
- Physical examination
- Explanation and planning
- Closing the session
Two threads run through the whole consultation rather than in sequence: providing structure (summarising, signposting, logical flow) and building the relationship (non-verbal behaviour, rapport, involving the patient).

Core skills
- Open questions first ("Tell me about what has been happening"), then focused and closed questions for detail ("Is it worse at night?"). This is often called the open-to-closed cone.
- Let the opening statement run. In a classic study, Beckman and Frankel (1984) found doctors interrupted patients' opening statements after an average of about 18 seconds, often before the patient had raised all their concerns.
- Active listening: attention, nodding, short prompts ("go on"), comfortable silence, and picking up verbal and non-verbal cues.
- Avoid leading questions ("You're not in pain, are you?") and stacked questions that ask several things at once.
- Summarise periodically and signpost changes of direction ("I'd now like to ask about your family, if that's alright").
- Show empathy: name and acknowledge the feeling ("That sounds frightening").

Ideas, concerns and expectations (ICE)
- Ideas: what the patient thinks is wrong or causing the problem.
- Concerns: what worries them about it.
- Expectations: what they hope will happen or want from the encounter.
Exploring ICE uncovers hidden worries (for example fear of cancer behind a cough), helps explanations fit the patient's frame, and supports shared decisions.

Giving information
- Chunk and check: give small amounts, then check understanding.
- Avoid jargon; use the patient's own words where you can.
- Teach-back: ask the patient to explain in their own words what they have understood. It checks your explanation, not their intelligence.

Barriers and how to deal with them
- Language: use a professional interpreter (in person, telephone or video). Avoid using family members, and especially children, because accuracy, confidentiality and the burden on the relative are all problems.
- Hearing loss: face the patient, reduce background noise, and use written notes or a British Sign Language interpreter if needed.
- Cognitive impairment or low health literacy: short sentences, one idea at a time, check understanding, and involve carers with consent.
- Emotional distress: slow down, acknowledge the emotion and allow silence.

Closing and afterwards
Thank the patient, summarise what you have learned, and make sure they are comfortable. In your tutorial, discuss what went well and what you would do differently, without identifiable details.

Exam tips: name the framework and its tasks precisely, give a sample phrase for each skill, and explain why the skill matters for accuracy, patient satisfaction or safety.

notes.h: Ethics, consent and mental capacity (England and Wales)
notes.body:
As a first-year student you will ask patients' permission to talk to them, sit in on consultations and visit their homes, so consent underpins everything you do. The law below applies in England and Wales; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own capacity legislation.

The four principles
Beauchamp and Childress (Principles of Biomedical Ethics, first edition 1979) proposed four principles:
- Respect for autonomy: a capable person's right to make their own decisions.
- Beneficence: acting in the patient's best interests.
- Non-maleficence: avoiding harm.
- Justice: fair distribution of benefits, risks and resources.
They often conflict, so the skill is weighing them in a specific case.

Valid consent
Consent is valid only if it is:
- given voluntarily, without coercion;
- informed, with the information a patient needs to decide;
- given by a person with capacity for that decision.
Consent may be express (spoken or written) or implied (holding out an arm for a blood pressure check). A signed form is evidence of a discussion, not proof of valid consent. Patients may withdraw consent at any time and can refuse to have students present without affecting their care.

How much must be disclosed?
- Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 replaced the approach in Sidaway (1985), which judged disclosure by what a responsible body of doctors would tell (the Bolam test).
- Doctors must take reasonable care to make sure the patient is aware of any material risks of a treatment and of reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor is or should reasonably be aware that this particular patient would.
- A narrow therapeutic exception applies where disclosure would seriously harm the patient's health; it must not be used to steer a patient.
- McCulloch v Forth Valley Health Board [2023] UKSC 26: which alternatives are reasonable is judged by professional standards (Bolam); materiality of risks stays patient-centred.
- GMC guidance, Decision making and consent (in effect from 9 November 2020), builds on this dialogue-based approach.

Mental Capacity Act 2005
Applies to people aged 16 and over.
- Section 1 principles: presume capacity; take all practicable steps to help the person decide; an unwise decision does not by itself mean a lack of capacity; anything done for a person who lacks capacity must be in their best interests; choose the least restrictive option.
- Section 2: a person lacks capacity if, at the material time, they cannot make the decision because of an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain. A diagnosis, age or appearance alone is not enough.
- Section 3 functional test: can the person understand the relevant information, retain it long enough, use or weigh it, and communicate the decision?
- Capacity is decision- and time-specific.
- Section 4 best interests: consider the person's past and present wishes, beliefs and values, and consult carers and others concerned with their welfare.
- A health and welfare lasting power of attorney or a valid, applicable advance decision to refuse treatment can bind decisions. Next of kin have no automatic power to consent for an adult.

Children and young people
- 16 and 17 year olds: section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969 lets them consent to treatment as if they were adults.
- Under 16s: under Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority [1986] AC 112 (House of Lords, 1985), a child can consent if they have enough understanding and intelligence to understand fully what is proposed ("Gillick competence").
- The Fraser guidelines from the same case cover contraception without parental knowledge: the young person understands the advice; cannot be persuaded to tell their parents or let the doctor tell them; is likely to have sex anyway; their physical or mental health is likely to suffer without it; and it is in their best interests.
- If a child lacks competence, a person with parental responsibility can usually consent.

Exam tips: quote the test, not just the case name; in capacity scenarios work through sections 2 and 3 in order and remember the "unwise decision" principle.

notes.h: Confidentiality, data protection and student professionalism
notes.body:
From your first placement you are trusted with personal information about patients. The GMC holds medical students to professional standards, and medical schools have their own fitness to practise procedures.

Professional standards for students
- Good medical practice is the GMC's core standard for doctors. The current version came into effect on 30 January 2024 and is organised into four domains: knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; and trust and professionalism.
- Achieving good medical practice is the GMC and Medical Schools Council guidance for medical students, updated in 2024 to reflect Good medical practice 2024. It expects students to behave professionally both on placement and in their private lives, including online.
- Typical concerns raised about students include dishonesty (for example in attendance records or assessments), poor attendance and engagement, inappropriate social media posts, and breaches of confidentiality. Honesty and insight usually matter as much as the original lapse.

Confidentiality
- The GMC guidance Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information came into effect on 25 April 2017.
- Confidentiality is not absolute. Disclosure can be justified when:
- the patient consents (implied consent is usually enough for sharing within the direct care team; express consent is needed for most other purposes);
- disclosure is required by law, such as notification of certain infectious diseases under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, or a court order;
- disclosure is justified in the public interest, where the benefit (usually preventing serious harm to others) outweighs the patient's and the public's interest in confidentiality.
- W v Egdell [1990] Ch 359 (Court of Appeal) upheld a psychiatrist's disclosure of a report about a dangerous patient to the authorities on public interest grounds.
- A standard example from GMC guidance: if a patient continues to drive against advice when not fit to do so, the doctor should, where possible, tell them first and should then contact the DVLA and disclose the relevant medical information in confidence.
- Wherever possible use anonymised information, and disclose only the minimum needed.

The Caldicott principles
Eight principles, the eighth added by the National Data Guardian in December 2020:
- 1 Justify the purpose; 2 use confidential information only when necessary; 3 use the minimum necessary; 4 access on a strict need-to-know basis; 5 everyone with access must understand their responsibilities; 6 comply with the law; 7 the duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty to protect confidentiality; 8 inform patients and service users about how their confidential information is used.

Data protection law
- In the UK, the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern personal data, as amended (including by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025).
- Health data are "special category" data, which need both a lawful basis and an additional condition for processing.
- Article 5 principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality (security); and accountability.
- Patients can make a subject access request to see their records; the usual time limit for a response is one month.
- Data protection law sits alongside, not instead of, the common law duty of confidence.

What this means for you on placement
- Never discuss patients where you can be overheard (lifts, cafes, public transport).
- Remove all identifiers from reflective writing, tutorial presentations and the survey project, including combinations of details (age, rare condition, street) that could identify someone.
- Never photograph patients or records on a personal phone, and never post about patients online.
- If you are worried about a patient's safety, tell your GP tutor rather than acting alone.

Exam tips: give the three bases for disclosure with an example of each, and link the Caldicott principles to a practical student scenario.

notes.h: General practice and primary care: GP clinics, home visits and reflection
notes.body:
Your Year 1 placement is based in a GP practice: Imperial's course page describes groups of four or eight students spending eight Thursdays there between October and March, with patient conversations, GP clinics, a community survey project and small-group tutorials. This topic gives you the background to make sense of what you see.

What primary care is
- Primary care is the first point of contact with the health service: general practice, community pharmacy, NHS dentistry and optometry.
- Barbara Starfield described four core functions of good primary care: first-contact access; continuity of care over time (longitudinality); comprehensiveness (dealing with most problems, of any body system, at any age); and coordination with other services.
- Countries with strong primary care tend to achieve better population health at lower cost, which is why the NHS relies on it.

How general practice is organised in England
- Most practices are independent contractors to the NHS (often partnerships) rather than NHS employees, working under national contracts (General Medical Services, Personal Medical Services or Alternative Provider Medical Services).
- People register with a practice, giving each practice a defined list. This makes continuity and population health work possible.
- Gatekeeping: GPs control access to most specialist hospital care through referral. This protects patients from unnecessary investigation, keeps specialist care for those who need it and controls costs.
- The Quality and Outcomes Framework (introduced in 2004) pays practices for meeting indicators, mainly in long-term conditions.
- Primary care networks (from July 2019) group neighbouring practices, typically covering 30,000 to 50,000 patients, and employ additional roles such as clinical pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and social prescribing link workers.

The practice team
GPs, practice nurses, healthcare assistants, pharmacists, receptionists and care navigators, and practice managers. Watch how tasks are shared and how information flows between them.

What to notice in GP clinics
- Undifferentiated problems: patients often present early, before a clear diagnosis is possible, so GPs manage uncertainty and use time as a diagnostic tool.
- Multimorbidity: many patients have several long-term conditions at once, so care is about the whole person rather than one organ.
- Continuity: a systematic review (Pereira Gray and colleagues, BMJ Open, 2018) found that continuity of care with doctors was associated with lower mortality.
- Consultation models: Roger Neighbour's The Inner Consultation (1987) describes five checkpoints: connecting, summarising, handing over, safety-netting and housekeeping (the doctor's own emotional readiness for the next patient).
- Safety-netting: telling the patient what to look out for, what to do if things change, and when to come back.
- Social prescribing: link workers connect patients with non-medical support such as community groups, debt advice or exercise programmes, which is the biopsychosocial model in action.

Home visits
Practices may arrange visits to patients who would benefit, often people who are housebound. You will see how housing, carers and isolation shape health, and the limits of what can be done outside a clinic. Always go as directed by the practice and follow its safety arrangements.

Reflection and tutorials
Small-group tutorials are where you make sense of experiences. A common structure is Gibbs' reflective cycle (Learning by Doing, 1988): description; feelings; evaluation; analysis; conclusion; action plan. Good reflection moves beyond describing events to analysing why things happened and what you will do differently.

Exam tips: use Starfield's four functions to structure answers on the value of primary care, and illustrate with concrete examples from placement (anonymised).

notes.h: The NHS in England: structure, funding and reform
notes.body:
PCH introduces the structure of the health service you will work in. Health is devolved, so NHS England, NHS Scotland, NHS Wales and Health and Social Care in Northern Ireland are organised differently. This note covers England as of October 2026.

Origins and principles
- The NHS was launched on 5 July 1948 under the National Health Service Act 1946, with Aneurin Bevan as Minister of Health.
- Founding principles: it meets the needs of everyone, it is free at the point of delivery, and it is based on clinical need, not ability to pay.
- The NHS Constitution for England (first published in 2009) sets out seven principles and patients' rights, including some waiting-time rights.

Funding
- Mainly funded from general taxation, with a contribution from National Insurance: a tax-funded, Beveridge-type system rather than social insurance.
- Some charges exist in England, such as prescription, dental and optical charges, with many exemptions. Prescriptions are free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
- Adult social care is separate: it is arranged by local authorities and is means-tested under the Care Act 2014. This boundary between free health care and means-tested social care causes many of the problems you will see at hospital discharge.

Who does what (England)
- Secretary of State for Health and Social Care and the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC): overall policy, funding and accountability to Parliament.
- NHS England: national leadership, commissioning oversight and performance management. In 2023 it absorbed NHS Digital and Health Education England.
- Integrated care systems (ICSs): put on a statutory footing by the Health and Care Act 2022 on 1 July 2022, when 42 were created and clinical commissioning groups (CCGs) were abolished. Each ICS has two statutory parts:
- the integrated care board (ICB), an NHS body that plans and commissions most local NHS services and holds the NHS budget for its population;
- the integrated care partnership (ICP), a joint committee of the ICB and local authorities that writes an integrated care strategy covering health, social care and wider determinants.
- ICSs have four aims: improve population health and health care outcomes; tackle inequalities in outcomes, experience and access; improve productivity and value for money; and help the NHS support broader social and economic development.
- On 1 April 2026 an NHS England order abolished 12 ICBs and created 6 new ones (one other ICB's boundary was widened), leaving 36 ICBs.
- Providers: NHS trusts and foundation trusts (acute, mental health, community, ambulance), GP practices, community pharmacies, and some independent providers.
- Regulation and guidance: the Care Quality Commission registers and inspects providers; NICE produces clinical and cost-effectiveness guidance; the GMC and NMC regulate professionals; the UK Health Security Agency (from 2021) leads on health protection.

A short history of reform
- 1990: the NHS and Community Care Act created an internal market, separating purchasers from providers.
- 2012: the Health and Social Care Act created CCGs, the NHS Commissioning Board (known as NHS England) and Public Health England, from April 2013, and emphasised competition.
- 2022: the Health and Care Act moved the emphasis from competition to collaboration and integration through ICSs.
- 3 July 2025: the government's 10 Year Health Plan for England, Fit for the Future, set out three shifts: from hospital to community, from analogue to digital, and from sickness to prevention.

NHS England's future
- On 13 March 2025 the government announced that NHS England would be abolished and its functions brought into DHSC.
- This needs legislation. The Health Bill 2026-27 was introduced in the Commons on 14 May 2026 and had its Commons second reading on 1 June 2026. By October 2026 it had passed the Commons and its Lords second reading, with Lords committee stage due to begin on 28 October 2026. It had not received Royal Assent, so NHS England still legally exists. Check the current position before your exams.

Exam tips: distinguish the ICB (budget and commissioning) from the ICP (strategy with local government), and do not describe CCGs as current.

notes.h: Health inequalities and the social determinants of health
notes.body:
Imperial's description of PCH stresses the social side of health and how it shapes patients' outcomes. In London you will see some of the sharpest health inequalities in the country within a few streets of each other.

Key definitions
- Health inequalities: systematic differences in health between groups of people. When they are avoidable and unfair, they are often called health inequities.
- Dimensions: socioeconomic position (income, education, occupation, area deprivation); geography; protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010 (such as age, disability, race and sex); and inclusion health groups such as people experiencing homelessness, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities, and vulnerable migrants.
- Social gradient: health does not just differ between the poorest and everyone else; it gets steadily better with each step up the social ladder. The Whitehall studies of British civil servants (Whitehall I from 1967, Whitehall II from 1985) showed higher mortality and disease at each lower employment grade.

How big are the gaps? (ONS, England, 2022 to 2024)
Comparing the most and least deprived tenths of areas (deciles of the Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025):
- Life expectancy at birth: males 73.2 v 83.6 years (a gap of 10.4 years); females 78.3 v 86.4 years (8.1 years).
- Healthy life expectancy at birth: males 49.8 v 69.2 years (19.4 years); females 48.2 v 68.5 years (20.3 years).
- So women in the most deprived areas can expect about 78.3 - 48.2 = 30.1 years in poor health, compared with 86.4 - 68.5 = 17.9 years in the least deprived areas.
- ONS also publishes the slope index of inequality, which uses the whole distribution: 10.4 and 8.0 years for life expectancy (males, females) and 19.3 and 20.1 years for healthy life expectancy.

Explaining the gaps
- Dahlgren and Whitehead's "rainbow" model (1991) places the individual (age, sex, genetic factors) at the centre, surrounded by layers of individual lifestyle factors; social and community networks; living and working conditions (education, work, unemployment, housing, water and sanitation, health care, food); and, outermost, general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions.
- The Black Report (1980) offered four explanations: artefact (a statistical illusion), natural or social selection (ill people drift down the social scale), cultural or behavioural (differences in smoking, diet and so on), and materialist or structural (income, housing and working conditions). It favoured the materialist explanation.
- Later reviews include the Acheson Inquiry (1998) and the Marmot Review, Fair Society, Healthy Lives (2010). Marmot set six policy objectives: give every child the best start in life; enable everyone to maximise their capabilities and have control over their lives; fair employment and good work for all; a healthy standard of living for all; healthy and sustainable places and communities; and stronger ill-health prevention. Health Equity in England: The Marmot Review 10 Years On (2020) reported that improvements in life expectancy had stalled and gaps had widened in some respects.
- Proportionate universalism (Marmot): actions should be universal, but with scale and intensity in proportion to the level of disadvantage.

Health care can make inequality worse
- The inverse care law (Julian Tudor Hart, Lancet, 1971): the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it in the population served.
- Barriers include language, digital access, inflexible working hours, cost of travel and previous poor experiences.

The NHS response
- NHS bodies have legal duties to have regard to reducing inequalities in access and outcomes.
- Core20PLUS5 (NHS England, 2021) targets the most deprived 20% of the national population by the Index of Multiple Deprivation (Core20), locally chosen PLUS groups, and five clinical areas for adults: maternity, severe mental illness, chronic respiratory disease, early cancer diagnosis, and hypertension case-finding with lipid management.

Exam tips: quote one up-to-date statistic accurately (state its source and years), distinguish life expectancy from healthy life expectancy, and link determinants to a real patient example.

notes.h: The community survey project: research methods and basic epidemiology
notes.body:
One of the four core activities of Year 1 PCH is a community survey project carried out with your practice; an earlier Imperial description (2019) gives patients' satisfaction with care or perceptions of health as typical subjects. Doing it well needs basic survey methods and epidemiology.

Designing the study
- Start with a focused research question, for example: "What proportion of adult patients at our practice find it difficult to get an appointment, and does this differ by age group?"
- A questionnaire survey at one point in time is a cross-sectional study. It measures prevalence and can show associations, but it cannot establish cause and effect or the order in which things happened.
- Define the target population (for example, registered adults) and the sampling frame (the list you actually sample from).

Sampling
- Probability methods: simple random sampling; systematic sampling (every nth person); stratified sampling (random samples within subgroups such as age bands); cluster sampling (randomly chosen groups).
- Non-probability methods: convenience sampling (whoever is in the waiting room), quota sampling, snowball sampling. These are quicker but more prone to bias. A waiting-room sample over-represents frequent attenders and misses people who cannot get appointments.
- Larger samples give more precise estimates, but a big biased sample is still biased.

Writing questions
- Closed questions (yes/no, multiple choice, Likert scales such as "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree") are easy to analyse; open questions give richer detail but take longer to analyse.
- Avoid leading questions, double-barrelled questions (asking two things at once), jargon, and vague time frames.
- Pilot the questionnaire on a few people first.
- Validity: does the question measure what it intends to? Reliability: does it give consistent results on repetition?

Bias
- Selection bias: the sample differs systematically from the target population.
- Non-response bias: people who reply differ from those who do not.
- Social desirability bias: people give answers they think are acceptable, especially when face to face with a medical student.
- Recall bias: inaccurate memory of past events.
- Interviewer bias: the way questions are asked influences answers.

Ethics and data
Explain the purpose, make participation voluntary, do not collect identifiable data unless essential, store responses securely, and follow your practice's guidance. This applies the data protection principles of data minimisation and security.

Analysing the results: a worked example
- 640 patients are invited and 400 respond. Response rate = 400 / 640 = 62.5%.
- 120 of the 400 respondents report difficulty getting an appointment. Proportion p = 120 / 400 = 0.30 (30%).
- Standard error = √[p(1 - p) / n] = √(0.30 × 0.70 / 400) = 0.0229.
- 95% confidence interval = p ± 1.96 × SE = 0.30 ± 0.045, so 25.5% to 34.5%.
- Interpretation: if the survey were repeated many times, about 95% of intervals calculated this way would contain the true proportion. The interval reflects random error only; it does not correct for bias.

Prevalence and incidence
- Prevalence = number of existing cases ÷ population at a given time. For example, 400 people with diabetes on a list of 8,000 gives a prevalence of 5%.
- Incidence = number of new cases ÷ population at risk over a stated period. If 38 new cases are diagnosed in a year among the 7,600 people without diabetes, incidence = 38 / 7,600 = 5.0 per 1,000 per year.
- For a stable, fairly rare condition, prevalence is approximately incidence × average duration. That is why long-lasting chronic diseases can have high prevalence even when incidence is modest.

Exam tips: always state the denominator and the time period, and say whether a survey result is a prevalence or an incidence.

notes.h: The hospital placement: secondary care and the patient pathway
notes.body:
PCH is not only about general practice. The 2026-27 programme specification says that in Years 1 and 2 students may see patients in homes, general practices and hospital settings, and that Year 1 contains the first clinical placement, where workplace-based assessments begin. The student union's Phase 1a guide describes placements in both primary and secondary care. This note gives the background for your time in hospital.

Levels of care
- Primary care: first contact (general practice, community pharmacy, dentistry, optometry).
- Secondary care: specialist care, usually in hospital, reached by referral or as an emergency (district general hospitals, mental health trusts).
- Tertiary care: highly specialised care, usually in regional or national centres, on referral from secondary care (for example complex cardiac surgery or specialist cancer treatment).
- Community and intermediate care: district nursing, rehabilitation and short-term "step-up" or "step-down" care designed to avoid admission or support discharge.

The patient pathway
- Planned (elective) route: the GP refers, often through the NHS e-Referral Service; outpatient assessment; diagnostics; treatment as a day case or inpatient; discharge back to the GP and community services.
- Urgent and emergency route: NHS 111, 999 and ambulance services, urgent treatment centres, emergency departments, and then admission or discharge.
- NHS Constitution standards include a right to start consultant-led treatment for non-urgent conditions within a maximum of 18 weeks from referral, and a standard that 95% of patients are admitted, transferred or discharged within four hours in A&E. National performance has fallen short of both for several years.
- Suspected cancer: the Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for patients to be told within 28 days of urgent referral whether or not they have cancer, and the 62-day standard covers urgent referral to first treatment.

Interfaces and fragmentation
- Many problems happen at transitions: incomplete discharge letters, medication changes not communicated, or delayed discharge while patients who are medically fit wait for social care or community support.
- Delayed discharge harms patients (deconditioning, hospital-acquired infection, loss of confidence) and reduces beds for new admissions.
- Integrated care systems and the "hospital to community" shift in the 10 Year Health Plan (July 2025) aim to reduce these gaps.

The multidisciplinary team
Doctors of all grades; nurses and healthcare assistants; pharmacists; physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech and language therapists and dietitians; social workers; discharge coordinators; porters and administrative staff. Note who does what and how decisions are communicated (ward rounds, handovers, MDT meetings).

Patient safety and quality
- The Francis Report (February 2013), on failings at Mid Staffordshire NHS Foundation Trust, emphasised a culture of openness, transparency and candour and putting patients first.
- Organisations have a statutory duty of candour (regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014); individual professionals have a professional duty of candour.
- Infection prevention: the World Health Organization's five moments for hand hygiene are before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching a patient's surroundings.

Being a student on the ward
Introduce yourself as a medical student, ask the patient's permission, respect their right to say no, wear identification, follow the hospital's infection control and dress policies, and raise any concerns about patient safety with your supervisor.

Exam tips: be able to trace one patient's journey through primary, secondary and community care, and identify where communication can fail.

questions.q: According to Talcott Parsons (1951), which of the following is an obligation, rather than a right, of the sick role?
options: Not to be held responsible for the illness
To receive care free at the point of use
To seek technically competent help and cooperate with it
To be excused from normal social duties
questions.why: Parsons gave the sick person two obligations: to want to get well and to seek technically competent help and cooperate with it. Being excused from normal social duties and not being blamed for the illness are the two rights of the sick role, so they are the classic mix-up with obligations. Care free at the point of use is a founding principle of the NHS (1948), not part of Parsons' sociological model, so it confuses a health-system principle with a social role.

questions.q: A woman with well-controlled epilepsy has never been treated unfairly because of it, but she hides her diagnosis from her employer and avoids social events because she fears rejection. Which concept best describes this?
options: Discredited stigma in Goffman's sense
Sanctioning, one of Zola's triggers
Felt stigma
Enacted stigma
questions.why: Felt stigma (Scambler and Hopkins, 1986) is the shame and fear of discrimination that leads people to conceal a condition, even when no one has discriminated against them. Enacted stigma needs actual discrimination, which has not happened here. Goffman's discredited person has a difference that is visible or already known; her epilepsy is hidden, so she is discreditable, not discredited. Sanctioning is Zola's trigger in which other people tell someone to consult a doctor, which is about deciding to seek care, not concealing a diagnosis.

questions.q: Using the biopsychosocial model, explain why two patients with the same diagnosis can have very different outcomes. Illustrate your answer with an example.
markScheme: Defines the biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977) and contrasts it with the biomedical model
Identifies relevant psychological factors (e.g. beliefs about illness, fear, mood, coping)
Identifies relevant social factors (e.g. employment, income, housing, family support)
Uses a concrete example in which the same pathology leads to different outcomes
Explains interaction between factors (e.g. fear leading to avoidance and deconditioning, or debt delaying rest)
questions.modelAnswer: The biomedical model explains illness by pathology alone, so it predicts that the same lesion gives the same outcome. Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) argues that biological, psychological and social factors interact. Take two people with the same knee osteoarthritis on X-ray. The first is a retired teacher with good support, who understands that activity is helpful and keeps walking; she stays fairly mobile. The second lives alone on a low income in a fourth-floor flat with no lift, believes exercise is 'wearing the joint out' and is low in mood. She moves less, loses muscle strength, becomes isolated and finds her pain harder to cope with. The same pathology therefore leads to very different disability. The factors also reinforce each other: fear leads to avoidance, avoidance to deconditioning and more pain, and isolation worsens mood. Good care therefore addresses beliefs, mood and social circumstances as well as the joint.

questions.q: You are starting a patient conversation in your GP practice. Which is the best opening question?
options: Is the pain sharp or dull?
You've come about your diabetes, haven't you?
How long have you had the pain, how often does it come and how bad is it?
Can you tell me about what has been happening with your health?
questions.why: An open question that invites the patient to tell their story is the best start, as in the open-to-closed cone of the Calgary-Cambridge approach. Asking whether the pain is sharp or dull is a closed, either-or question, useful later for detail but it narrows the conversation too early. Saying 'You've come about your diabetes, haven't you?' is a leading question that assumes the agenda and may stop the patient raising other concerns. Asking how long, how often and how bad in one breath is a stacked question; the patient can only answer one part at a time and parts get lost.

questions.q: A patient with very limited English attends with her 12-year-old son, who offers to interpret. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Arrange a professional interpreter, in person or by telephone or video
Let the son interpret because he is family and the patient agrees
Carry on in English, speaking slowly and using gestures
Ask her to come back another day with an adult relative to interpret
questions.why: A professional interpreter gives accurate translation, protects confidentiality and avoids burdening a child, so this is the standard of good practice. Using the son assumes that family members are a safe default; in fact he may filter or mistranslate, the patient may not disclose sensitive information in front of him, and it places an inappropriate burden on a child. Carrying on in slow English with gestures assumes understanding that may not be there and risks serious misunderstanding. Sending her away to find an adult relative delays care and still relies on an untrained family interpreter, with the same accuracy and confidentiality problems.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by ICE in a consultation and give two reasons why exploring it is important.
markScheme: Ideas: what the patient thinks is wrong or causing the problem
Concerns: what the patient is worried about
Expectations: what the patient hopes will happen or wants from the visit
Any two valid reasons: uncovers hidden worries; lets explanations fit the patient's beliefs; supports shared decision-making and adherence; improves satisfaction and avoids mismatched expectations
questions.modelAnswer: ICE stands for ideas, concerns and expectations. Ideas are what the patient believes is going on (for example 'I think it's my heart'). Concerns are what worries them about it (perhaps that they will end up like a parent who died of a heart attack). Expectations are what they want from the encounter, such as a test, reassurance or a referral. Exploring ICE matters because it often uncovers a hidden worry that would otherwise go unaddressed, and because an explanation that starts from the patient's own understanding is more likely to be believed and remembered. It also supports shared decision-making: if a patient expects antibiotics and the clinician does not think they will help, knowing this allows an honest discussion rather than a frustrating mismatch.

questions.q: A 79-year-old woman with mild dementia declines a recommended hip operation, saying she would rather use a walking frame. She understands the information, remembers it, weighs the risks and benefits and clearly communicates her choice. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what follows?
options: Her children can consent to the operation on her behalf as next of kin
She has capacity for this decision and her refusal must be respected, even if the team thinks it unwise
She lacks capacity because she has a diagnosis of dementia
She lacks capacity because refusing beneficial surgery is an unwise decision
questions.why: She passes the section 3 functional test (understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate), and capacity is presumed under section 1, so her refusal stands. Treating the dementia diagnosis as decisive is wrong because the Act says a condition alone does not establish incapacity; the question is whether she can make this particular decision. Treating her refusal as proof of incapacity ignores section 1(4): an unwise decision does not by itself show a lack of capacity. Relying on her children as next of kin is wrong because next of kin have no legal power to consent for an adult; only an attorney under a valid health and welfare lasting power of attorney or a court-appointed deputy can decide on an adult's behalf, and only if she lacked capacity; otherwise the clinician would decide in her best interests under section 4, consulting her family.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the test for disclosing risks set out in Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11?
options: Doctors must disclose any material risk: one a reasonable person in the patient's position would think significant, or one this patient would, as the doctor knows or should know
Doctors must disclose whatever a responsible body of medical opinion would disclose
Doctors must disclose every possible risk, however rare
Doctors need only disclose risks with a probability above 1%
questions.why: Montgomery adopted a patient-centred materiality test with an objective limb (the reasonable patient) and a subjective limb (this particular patient). Relying on what a responsible body of doctors would disclose is the Bolam/Sidaway approach that Montgomery replaced for risk disclosure, so it is out of date. Listing every possible risk misunderstands the case: the duty is to disclose material risks through dialogue, not to overwhelm the patient with every remote possibility. A fixed 1% cut-off is wrong because the Supreme Court said materiality cannot be reduced to percentages; it depends on the nature of the risk and on what matters to the patient.

questions.q: A 15-year-old asks her GP for contraception and does not want her parents to know. Outline the legal and ethical framework the GP should apply in England.
markScheme: Under-16s can consent if Gillick competent (Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986] AC 112, HL)
Fraser guidelines for contraception: understands; will not involve parents; likely to have sex anyway; health likely to suffer without it; best interests
Encourage (but do not require) her to involve her parents
Confidentiality is owed to her as to an adult, but may be breached where there is a safeguarding concern (e.g. exploitation, abuse, coercion)
Ethical balance: respect for autonomy versus beneficence and protection from harm
questions.modelAnswer: At 15 she cannot rely on section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969, which covers 16 and 17 year olds, so the question is whether she is Gillick competent: does she have enough understanding and intelligence to understand fully what is proposed? For contraception specifically, the GP should apply the Fraser guidelines from the same House of Lords case: she understands the advice; she cannot be persuaded to tell her parents or allow the GP to tell them; she is likely to have sex with or without contraception; her physical or mental health is likely to suffer without it; and providing it is in her best interests. The GP should encourage her to involve a parent or trusted adult but cannot insist. Her confidentiality should be respected in the same way as an adult's. The exception is safeguarding: if there are signs of abuse, exploitation or a much older or coercive partner, the GP may need to share information with safeguarding services, ideally telling her first. Ethically, this balances respect for her developing autonomy against the duty to protect her from harm.

questions.q: You want to write about a memorable patient from your GP placement in a reflective piece for your tutor. What should you do?
options: Include the patient's name, because they agreed to talk to you
Remove anything that could identify the patient, including combinations of details such as age, rare condition and street
Use only the patient's initials, which makes the account anonymous
Include identifying details, because only tutors bound by confidentiality will read it
questions.why: Reflective writing should be fully anonymised, and identifiability can come from a combination of details, not just a name; this follows the minimum-necessary principle. Initials are still identifying, especially together with age and condition, so using them is not anonymisation. The fact that readers owe confidentiality does not justify sharing identifiable data they do not need; Caldicott principles 3 and 4 limit use to the minimum necessary and need-to-know. Agreeing to a conversation is not consent to being named in written coursework, so relying on that agreement confuses consent for one purpose with consent for another.

questions.q: Which of these disclosures is justified mainly on public interest grounds?
options: Telling the patient's employer about his diagnosis because the employer phoned to ask
Informing the DVLA after a patient with uncontrolled seizures continues to drive despite being advised to stop
Notifying a case of measles under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010
Sharing the record with the practice nurse who is dressing the patient's leg ulcer
questions.why: Disclosing to the DVLA when a patient keeps driving while unfit is the GMC's classic public interest example: the risk of serious harm to others outweighs confidentiality. Notifying measles is a disclosure required by law under the 2010 Regulations, so it rests on a legal duty, not on a public interest judgement. Sharing with the nurse treating the ulcer is sharing within the direct care team on the basis of implied consent. Telling the employer has no valid basis at all: there is no consent, no legal requirement and no risk of serious harm, so an employer's request alone never justifies disclosure.

questions.q: Describe three circumstances in which a doctor may disclose confidential patient information, giving an example of each.
markScheme: Consent: implied consent for direct care (e.g. referral letter to a specialist); express consent for other purposes (e.g. insurance report)
Required by law: e.g. notifiable disease under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, or a court order
Public interest: e.g. telling the DVLA about a patient who continues to drive while unfit; W v Egdell [1990]
Disclose the minimum necessary, use anonymised data where possible, and inform the patient where safe and practicable
Refers to GMC Confidentiality guidance (in effect 25 April 2017)
questions.modelAnswer: GMC guidance (Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information, in effect from 25 April 2017) recognises three main bases for disclosure. First, consent. Implied consent covers sharing within the team providing direct care, such as a GP sending relevant history to a hospital specialist on referral. Express consent is needed for most other purposes, such as a report for an insurer. Second, disclosure required by law. A doctor must notify suspected cases of certain infectious diseases, such as measles, under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, and must comply with a court order. Third, disclosure in the public interest, where the benefits, usually preventing a risk of death or serious harm to others, outweigh the interest in confidentiality. An example is informing the DVLA when a patient with uncontrolled epilepsy keeps driving despite advice; in W v Egdell (1990) the Court of Appeal upheld disclosure of a psychiatric report about a dangerous patient on this basis. In every case the doctor should disclose only the minimum necessary, use anonymised data where that will do, and usually tell the patient first unless that would be unsafe.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the gatekeeping role of general practice in the NHS?
options: GPs control access to most specialist hospital care through referral
Receptionists triage requests to decide which patients get an appointment
Integrated care boards decide which services to commission for their population
Patients can refer themselves directly to any hospital specialist
questions.why: Gatekeeping means the GP acts as the route into most specialist care, which is what the GP referral statement says. Receptionist triage is care navigation within the practice; it controls access to the GP, not to specialist care, so it takes the word 'gatekeeping' too literally. ICB commissioning decides which services exist and are funded, which is a planning role rather than a clinician controlling an individual's access. Unrestricted self-referral to specialists is the opposite of gatekeeping and describes systems without it.

questions.q: In Gibbs' reflective cycle, which stage comes directly after 'description' and 'feelings'?
options: Conclusion
Action plan
Evaluation
Analysis
questions.why: The order is description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan, so evaluation (what was good and bad about the experience) comes third. Analysis (making sense of why things happened) is the fourth stage and is often put too early because it sounds like the natural next step. Conclusion is the fifth stage, drawing together what you have learned. Action plan is the final stage, what you would do next time, so choosing it skips the reflective middle of the cycle.

questions.q: Using Starfield's four core functions of primary care, explain why general practice is important to the NHS.
markScheme: First-contact access: an accessible first point of contact for new problems
Continuity (longitudinality): ongoing relationship over time; associated with better outcomes including lower mortality
Comprehensiveness: deals with most problems across all ages and body systems, including multimorbidity
Coordination: links and coordinates care with hospitals, community and social services; gatekeeping protects resources
questions.modelAnswer: Starfield identified four functions that explain the value of primary care. First-contact access means the GP practice is the usual first place people go with a new problem, so most problems are dealt with close to home and early. Continuity, or longitudinality, means an ongoing relationship with a registered list of patients over years; continuity of doctor care has been associated with lower mortality, and it builds trust and knowledge of the patient's context. Comprehensiveness means general practice deals with almost any problem at any age, which suits the many patients with multimorbidity. Coordination means the GP joins up care, referring to and receiving information from hospitals, community services and social care; gatekeeping also keeps specialist resources for those who need them. Together these let the NHS deliver most care efficiently and in a way centred on the whole person.

questions.q: Since 1 July 2022, which body plans and commissions most local NHS services and holds the NHS budget for its population in England?
options: The integrated care board
The clinical commissioning group
The integrated care partnership
The Care Quality Commission
questions.why: The integrated care board is the statutory NHS body in each integrated care system that holds the budget and commissions most services. Clinical commissioning groups did this from 2013 but were abolished on 1 July 2022, so choosing them is an out-of-date answer. The integrated care partnership is the other half of the system, a joint committee with local authorities that writes the integrated care strategy; it does not hold the NHS budget, so choosing it confuses the two parts of an ICS. The Care Quality Commission is a regulator that inspects providers and does not commission services.

questions.q: What change to NHS England did the government announce on 13 March 2025?
options: It would be merged into the Care Quality Commission
It would be renamed the NHS Commissioning Board
It would become an arm's-length body independent of ministers for the first time
It would be abolished and its functions brought into the Department of Health and Social Care
questions.why: The March 2025 announcement was that NHS England would be abolished and its work brought into DHSC, which needs legislation (the Health Bill 2026-27). A merger into the Care Quality Commission confuses this with a different proposal in the same Bill, which would merge the Health Services Safety Investigations Body into the CQC. 'NHS Commissioning Board' was the body's original legal name under the 2012 Act, so this reverses history rather than describing a reform. NHS England has been an arm's-length body since 2013, and the 2025 plan moves it closer to ministers, not further away, so the last statement gets the direction of change backwards.

questions.q: Describe the structure of an integrated care system in England and explain what the Health and Care Act 2022 was intended to change.
markScheme: ICSs made statutory on 1 July 2022 (42 created); CCGs abolished
ICB: NHS body that commissions most local NHS services and holds the budget
ICP: joint committee of ICB and local authorities that produces an integrated care strategy
Aims include improving outcomes, tackling inequalities, value for money, wider social and economic development
Shift from competition (2012 Act) to collaboration and integration between NHS, local government and other partners
questions.modelAnswer: The Health and Care Act 2022 put integrated care systems on a statutory footing on 1 July 2022, when 42 were created across England and clinical commissioning groups were abolished. Each ICS has two statutory parts. The integrated care board is an NHS body that plans and commissions most local NHS services and holds the NHS budget for its population. The integrated care partnership is a joint committee of the ICB and the local authorities in its area; it produces an integrated care strategy that covers health, social care and wider determinants such as housing. ICSs aim to improve population health and outcomes, tackle inequalities in outcomes, experience and access, improve productivity and value for money, and help the NHS support wider social and economic development. The Act was intended to move away from the competition and purchaser-provider emphasis of the Health and Social Care Act 2012 towards collaboration, with NHS organisations, councils and others planning together for a whole population rather than competing for contracts.

questions.q: According to ONS figures for England in 2022 to 2024, roughly how large was the gap in healthy life expectancy at birth for females between the most and least deprived deciles?
options: About 30 years
About 48 years
About 20 years
About 8 years
questions.why: Healthy life expectancy was 48.2 years in the most deprived decile and 68.5 years in the least, a gap of 20.3 years (the slope index of inequality was 20.1 years). About 8 years is the gap in total life expectancy for females (78.3 v 86.4 years), so it confuses life expectancy with healthy life expectancy. About 30 years is the time women in the most deprived areas can expect to live in poor health (78.3 - 48.2 = 30.1 years), a comparison within one decile rather than between deciles. About 48 years is the healthy life expectancy value itself in the most deprived decile, read as if it were the gap.

questions.q: Which statement describes the inverse care law?
options: Each extra pound spent on health care produces a smaller gain in health
Universal services should be delivered with intensity proportionate to disadvantage
The availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it in the population served
Health tends to improve step by step as social position rises
questions.why: Julian Tudor Hart's inverse care law (1971) is that those who most need good care are least likely to get it. Health improving with social position is the social gradient in health, which describes outcomes rather than the distribution of care. Smaller health gains from each extra pound is the economic idea of diminishing marginal returns, not Tudor Hart's observation about who receives care. Delivering universal services with intensity proportionate to disadvantage is Marmot's proportionate universalism, a proposed remedy for inequalities rather than a description of the problem.

questions.q: A family of five lives in an overcrowded, damp privately rented flat in a deprived London borough. Using the Dahlgren and Whitehead model, explain how social determinants could contribute to poorer health for this family.
markScheme: Names and explains the layered model (Dahlgren and Whitehead, 1991)
Living and working conditions: damp and overcrowding (respiratory illness, infection spread, poor sleep, stress)
Socioeconomic conditions: low income, insecure tenancy, limits on diet, heating and activity
Social and community networks: isolation or support; access to services (inverse care law)
Links to lifestyle factors and outcomes, e.g. stress, smoking or poor diet as responses to circumstances rather than free choices
questions.modelAnswer: Dahlgren and Whitehead's model (1991) places the individual's age, sex and genes at the centre, surrounded by layers of lifestyle factors, social and community networks, living and working conditions, and wider socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions. For this family, the living conditions layer is most obvious: damp and mould are linked to respiratory problems such as asthma, overcrowding helps infections spread and disrupts sleep and children's homework, and an insecure private tenancy causes chronic stress. In the outer layer, low income and high London housing costs limit spending on heating and healthy food, and may push parents into insecure or shift work. Social and community networks may be thin if the family has moved often, increasing isolation, and services may be hard to reach, as the inverse care law predicts. These conditions shape behaviour: smoking, poor diet or inactivity are often responses to stress and constraint rather than free choices. The model therefore suggests that housing, income and community support matter as much as individual advice.

questions.q: In a practice survey, 640 patients are invited and 400 respond. Of the respondents, 120 report difficulty getting an appointment. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the proportion reporting difficulty?
questions.why: p = 120/400 = 0.30 and SE = √(0.30 × 0.70 / 400) = 0.0229, so the interval is 0.30 ± 1.96 × 0.0229 = 25.5% to 34.5%. The interval of 26.4% to 33.6% comes from putting the 640 people invited into the standard error instead of the 400 who answered, which makes the estimate look more precise than it is. The interval of 27.7% to 32.3% is 0.30 ± one standard error, forgetting to multiply by 1.96, so it is only about a 68% interval. The interval of 15.7% to 21.8% uses 120/640 = 18.75% as the proportion, wrongly counting non-responders as if they had said they had no difficulty.

questions.q: A draft survey question reads: 'How satisfied are you with the practice's opening hours and the friendliness of the reception staff?' What is the main problem with it?
options: It is a leading question that pushes respondents towards a particular answer
It is an open question whose answers will be hard to analyse
It will cause recall bias because it asks about events long ago
It is double-barrelled: it asks about two things at once
questions.why: The question combines opening hours and staff friendliness, so a patient who likes one and not the other cannot answer meaningfully, which is the definition of a double-barrelled question. It is not leading, because the wording does not suggest that the respondent should be satisfied or dissatisfied. It is not an open question, since 'how satisfied' would normally be answered on a closed rating scale such as a Likert scale. Recall bias concerns inaccurate memory of past events; this asks about current satisfaction with no distant time frame, so recall is not the main flaw.

questions.q: A GP practice has 8,000 registered patients. On 1 January, 400 of them have a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. During the following year, 38 new cases are diagnosed. (a) Calculate the prevalence on 1 January. (b) Calculate the annual incidence per 1,000 people at risk. (c) Explain why the two measures answer different questions.
markScheme: (a) Prevalence = 400 / 8,000 = 5%
(b) Population at risk = 8,000 - 400 = 7,600
(b) Incidence = 38 / 7,600 = 5.0 per 1,000 per year (no credit for using 8,000 as the denominator, which gives 4.75)
(c) Prevalence measures burden at a point in time (useful for planning services); incidence measures the rate of new cases (risk, causes, effect of prevention)
(c) Prevalence is approximately incidence × duration, so a long-lasting condition can have high prevalence
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Prevalence is existing cases divided by the population at that time: 400 / 8,000 = 0.05, or 5%. (b) Incidence uses new cases over a period divided by the population at risk. The 400 people who already have diabetes cannot develop it again, so the population at risk is 8,000 - 400 = 7,600. Incidence = 38 / 7,600 = 0.0050 per year, or 5.0 per 1,000 per year. Using the whole list of 8,000 as the denominator would give 4.75 per 1,000, which slightly underestimates the risk. (c) Prevalence tells you how much disease there is at a given time, which is what a practice needs to plan clinics, nurse time and medication reviews. Incidence tells you how quickly new cases are arising, which is what you need to study causes or judge whether prevention is working. The two are linked: for a stable condition, prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by average duration, so a lifelong condition like type 2 diabetes builds up a high prevalence even if incidence is modest.

questions.q: A patient is referred from a district general hospital to a regional specialist centre for complex cardiac surgery. What level of care is the specialist centre providing?
options: Secondary care
Primary care
Intermediate care
Tertiary care
questions.why: Highly specialised care in a regional or national centre, reached on referral from secondary care, is tertiary care. The district general hospital provided secondary care, so choosing secondary care stops at the previous step of the pathway. Primary care is first-contact care such as general practice, which the patient has already moved beyond. Intermediate care is short-term step-up or step-down support, often rehabilitation, to avoid admission or help discharge, not specialist surgery.

questions.q: Under the NHS Constitution for England, within what maximum time from referral do patients have a right to start consultant-led treatment for a non-urgent condition?
options: 4 hours
28 days
62 days
18 weeks
questions.why: The NHS Constitution gives a right to start consultant-led treatment within a maximum of 18 weeks from referral for non-urgent conditions. Four hours is the A&E standard for admission, transfer or discharge, so it mixes up emergency and elective care. Twenty-eight days is the cancer Faster Diagnosis Standard for telling patients whether they have cancer, which concerns diagnosis, not starting treatment. Sixty-two days is the cancer standard from urgent referral to first treatment, which applies only to suspected cancer, not to non-urgent referrals.

questions.q: An 84-year-old woman who lives alone is admitted with a hip fracture after a fall. Outline her likely journey through primary, secondary and community care, and identify two points where care could become fragmented.
markScheme: Emergency route: ambulance (999), emergency department, admission under a specialist team (secondary care)
Inpatient care by the multidisciplinary team (surgeons, physicians, nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, social workers)
Discharge planning involving community services, intermediate care or rehabilitation, and social care (means-tested, local authority)
Return to primary care: GP follow-up, medication review, falls prevention
Two valid fragmentation points, e.g. delayed discharge waiting for social care; incomplete or late discharge information to the GP; medication changes not communicated
questions.modelAnswer: She is likely to arrive by ambulance after a 999 call and be assessed in the emergency department before admission under a specialist team, which is secondary care. In hospital a multidisciplinary team is involved: surgeons for the operation, physicians or orthogeriatricians for her general health, nurses, physiotherapists and occupational therapists for mobility and daily living, and social workers and discharge coordinators to plan her return home. Because she lives alone, she may need intermediate care or rehabilitation, adaptations at home and a package of social care, which is arranged by the local authority and means-tested under the Care Act 2014. After discharge, her GP and community teams take over: medication review, wound and pain management, falls and bone health assessment, and checking how she is coping. Care can fragment at several points. If social care is not ready, she may remain in hospital when medically fit (delayed discharge), losing mobility and risking infection. If the discharge summary is late or incomplete, the GP may not know about medication changes or follow-up plans, creating safety risks.

questions.q: 'The NHS cannot close the gap in healthy life expectancy between rich and poor areas on its own.' Discuss, drawing on evidence about the social determinants of health and on examples from primary care.
markScheme: Defines health inequalities and distinguishes life expectancy from healthy life expectancy; cites accurate current data (e.g. ONS 2022-24: female HLE 48.2 v 68.5 years; male 49.8 v 69.2)
Explains the social gradient and determinants using a named framework (Dahlgren and Whitehead 1991; Black Report 1980 explanations; Marmot 2010)
Argues that most determinants (income, housing, education, work) lie outside the NHS, so cross-sector action is needed (Marmot's six objectives; proportionate universalism)
Recognises what the NHS can do: inverse care law means health care can widen gaps; proactive primary care, Core20PLUS5, outreach, social prescribing, prevention
Discusses structural levers that link NHS and wider partners: integrated care partnerships with local authorities; ICS aim to tackle inequalities
Uses concrete primary care examples (e.g. hypertension case-finding in deprived populations, interpreter use, home visits)
Reaches a balanced, justified conclusion
Clear structure, accurate terminology, evidence correctly attributed
questions.modelAnswer:
Health inequalities are systematic differences in health between groups; where avoidable and unfair they are inequities. The gap in healthy life expectancy (years lived in good health) is even wider than the gap in life expectancy. ONS figures for England in 2022 to 2024 show healthy life expectancy of 48.2 years for women in the most deprived decile against 68.5 years in the least deprived, a gap of about 20 years, while the life expectancy gap for women was about 8 years.

The statement is largely right because most causes of this gap lie outside health care. Dahlgren and Whitehead's model (1991) places health care as just one of many living and working conditions, alongside housing, education, work and income, all set within wider socioeconomic conditions. The Black Report (1980) favoured materialist explanations, and the Marmot Review (2010) argued that action is needed across the life course, with six objectives from early childhood to healthy places, few of which the NHS controls. Damp housing, insecure work and low income produce illness faster than a GP can treat it. The social gradient seen in the Whitehall studies also shows that inequality affects everyone below the top, not just the poorest, so it is fundamentally social.

However, the NHS is not powerless, and it can make things worse. Tudor Hart's inverse care law (1971) warns that good care is least available where it is most needed, so an NHS that waits for patients to come will widen gaps. Proactive primary care can narrow them: Core20PLUS5 targets the most deprived 20% and conditions such as hypertension, where case-finding and treatment in deprived areas prevent strokes and heart attacks. Practices can use interpreters, offer flexible appointments, do home visits and use social prescribing to connect patients with debt advice or housing support. Following Marmot, proportionate universalism means offering services to everyone but with more effort where need is greater.

The NHS also has structural ways to work with others. Integrated care partnerships bring ICBs together with local authorities, which run housing, public health and social care, and tackling inequalities is one of the four aims of integrated care systems.

In conclusion, the NHS cannot close the gap alone, because the main drivers are social and economic. But it has a real role in avoiding the inverse care law, delivering targeted prevention and acting as an advocate and partner in cross-sector action.

questions.q: Mr K, aged 82, lives alone and has a diagnosis of mild dementia. During a home visit you attend with the GP, the GP recommends referral for investigation of unexplained weight loss. Mr K's daughter takes you aside and asks that her father not be told anything that might upset him. (a) How should the GP decide whether Mr K has capacity to decide about the referral? (6 marks) (b) What must Mr K be told to give valid consent, and how does Montgomery apply? (6 marks) (c) How should the GP respond to the daughter's request, with reference to confidentiality? (4 marks) (d) Identify biopsychosocial factors relevant to Mr K's care. (4 marks)
markScheme: (a) MCA 2005 s1: presume capacity; all practicable steps to help (time, simple language, written aids, good time of day); unwise decision not evidence of incapacity

(a) s2: impairment or disturbance of mind or brain (dementia) AND s3 functional test: understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate; decision-specific and time-specific; dementia diagnosis alone insufficient
(a) If he lacks capacity: s4 best interests, consult daughter and consider his past wishes; check for LPA

(b) Valid consent: voluntary, informed, capacity. Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11: material risks and reasonable alternatives (including not investigating), judged by reasonable patient and this patient; GMC Decision making and consent (2020)
(b) Therapeutic exception is narrow; a relative's wish to protect him is not a ground for withholding information
(c) Duty of confidentiality is owed to Mr K; the daughter cannot veto disclosure to him or receive information without his consent; explore her concerns and involve her with his agreement

(d) Biological: weight loss, possible malignancy, dementia, frailty. Psychological: anxiety, mood, understanding. Social: lives alone, nutrition, support from daughter, access to transport for hospital appointments
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 the GP must start by presuming that Mr K has capacity (section 1(2)) and take all practicable steps to help him decide: a quiet setting, a good time of day, simple language, written information and time to think. Capacity is decision-specific, so the question is only whether he can decide about this referral now. The GP applies section 2: is there an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain? Dementia qualifies, but the diagnosis alone is not enough. Under section 3 he lacks capacity only if, because of that impairment, he cannot understand the relevant information, retain it long enough, use or weigh it, or communicate a decision. If he refuses, an unwise decision does not in itself show incapacity. If he does lack capacity, the GP must act in his best interests under section 4, considering his past wishes and values, consulting his daughter, and checking whether there is a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare.

(b) Valid consent must be voluntary, informed and given with capacity. Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11, the GP must take reasonable care to make sure he knows the material risks and reasonable alternatives, including the option of not investigating. A risk is material if a reasonable person in his position would attach significance to it, or if the GP knows or should know that Mr K would. This should be a dialogue, in line with GMC Decision making and consent (2020): what matters to him, such as staying at home, shapes what he needs to know. The therapeutic exception is narrow and does not allow information to be withheld simply because a relative thinks it will upset him.

(c) The duty of confidentiality is owed to Mr K, not his daughter. She cannot decide what he is told, and information about him should be shared with her only with his consent (or in his best interests if he lacks capacity). The GP should acknowledge her worries, explain this kindly, and offer to involve her in discussions if her father agrees.

(d) Biologically, weight loss may reflect cancer, other illness or poor nutrition, and dementia and frailty affect what investigations he can tolerate. Psychologically, he may be anxious or low in mood and his understanding may vary. Socially, he lives alone, so cooking, shopping, transport to hospital appointments and his daughter's support all affect both the cause of his weight loss and the feasibility of investigation.
